quotes.text: Australian writer Glenn A. Baker described how they used their "undeniably American laid-back style" to provide "six Stateside top ten hits", which are included on this compilation.

He considered the songs' writers, aside from band member Graham Russell, who "continued to pen excellent commercial songs, outside hitwriters (such as Lee Greenwood and the legendary Howie Greenfield) were also engaged to keep the hits flowing."
Australian writer Glenn A. Baker described how they used their "undeniably American laid-back style" to provide "six Stateside top ten hits", which are included on this compilation.

He considered the songs' writers, aside from band member Graham Russell, who "continued to pen excellent commercial songs, outside hitwriters (such as Lee Greenwood and the legendary Howie Greenfield) were also engaged to keep the hits flowing."

The title track opens with a mix of the classic singer/songwriter format that the 1970s brought music with Paul Simon, Linda Ronstadt, and James Taylor, before the rest of the band comes in during the chorus with its pop sound.

Themes of relationships of love, friendships, and longing have been staples of the group's music since the heyday of the chart hits in the '80s like "Making Love Out Of Nothing At All" (written by the great Jim Steinman), "All Out Of Love," and "Just As I Am."
For many, Air Supply was known for just light rock adult contemporary love songs, but overlook the musicality of the backing musicians in their band from the beginning.

The song "I Want Your Love" is an example of this release, with its blues/rock guitar-driven rhythms that should be a single. It isn't too heavy for pop, but not light or sappy for the critics who dismiss the band.

"Lovers" and the closing "We'll Meet Again" have two separate Beatles-influenced sounds, with the first a throwback to the Let It Be era, a la "Two Of Us," and the latter an Abbey Road sound with vocal effects and a pop-psychedelic mix that are gems on the album.

Producer Brian Howes (Simple Plan, Skillet, Men Without Hats) helps give singers Graham Russell and Russell Hitchcock a modern sound, without shying away from the signature format that their fans expect from them.
